rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the two nūn readings, the clause about what they do with their wealth coordinates with what their fathers worship, meaning they ask whether to abandon it and keep their practices.
rows.anchor: فمن قرأ بالنون فيهما فقوله: أو أن نفعل معطوف على قوله: ما يعبد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With tāʾ in both verbs, or nūn in both, the clause coordinates with ‘leave’: Shuʿayb commands them to leave ancestral worship and, by the readings, their own or his conduct with wealth.
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ بالتاء فيهما أو بالنون فيهما فمعطوف على أن نترك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disjunctive particle indicates variation, as Shuʿayb commands one thing at one time and another at another; another view gives it the sense of ‘and.’
rows.anchor: وأو للتنويع أي: تأمرك مرة بهذا، ومرة بهذا. وقيل: بمعنى الواو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent meaning of their conduct with wealth is the previously mentioned short measure and weight.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الذي كانوا يفعلونه في أموالهم هو بخس الكيل والوزن المقدم ذكره

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn Kaʿb says they clipped dinars and dirhams, then passed them off alongside sound coins as fraud.
rows.anchor: وقال محمد بن كعب: قرضهم الدينار والدرهم، وإجراء ذلك مع الصحيح على جهة التدليس

rows.speaker: ابن المسيب
rows.claim: Ibn al-Musayyib regards cutting dinars and dirhams as corruption in the land.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن المسيب: قطع الدنانير والدراهم من الفساد في الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view identifies the misconduct as changing currency types in order to consume people's property unlawfully.
rows.anchor: وقيل: تبديل السكك التي يقصد بها أكل أموال الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With tāʾ in both verbs or in ‘we wish,’ the apparent reading is that Shuʿayb required full measure and weight; Sufyan al-Thawri instead says he ordered almsgiving.
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ بالتاء فيهما أو في نشاء، والظاهر أنه إيفاء المكيال والميزان. وقال سفيان الثوري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their description of Shuʿayb as forbearing and right-minded may be sincere praise, challenging how such a person could oppose ancestral religion.
rows.anchor: فيحتمل أن يريدوا بذلك الحقيقة أي: إنك للمتصف بهذين الوصفين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The words may mean ‘forbearing and right-minded by your own claim,’ since he commands them as he does.
rows.anchor: أو يحتمل أن يريدوا بذلك إنك لأنت الحليم الرشيد بزعمك

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada reads the compliment as mockery and sarcasm, implying that Shuʿayb is actually rash and foolish.
rows.anchor: أن قالوا ذلك على سبيل الاستهزاء والتهكم، قاله قتادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their apparent praise indirectly imputes rashness and foolishness, like calling a miser generous or an Abyssinian ‘father of the white one.’
rows.anchor: والمراد: نسبته إلى الطيش والعي كما تقول للشحيح: لو رآك حاتم لسجد لك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shuʿayb's reply is a subtle, gentle appeal meant to win them over and draw them down from opposition.
rows.anchor: يا قوم أرأيتم إن كنت هذه مراجعة لطيفة واستنزال حسن، واستدعاء رقيق

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet called Shuʿayb ‘the orator of the prophets.’
rows.anchor: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «ذلك خطيب الأنبياء»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rhetoricians call this technique drawing the addressee in; it is a subtle way to reach one's aim, also found in the stories of Abraham, Noah, Hud, Salih, and the believer from Pharaoh's people.
rows.anchor: وهذا النوع يسمى استدراج المخاطب عند أرباب علم البيان، وهو نوع لطيف غريب المغزى

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says the answer to ‘Have you considered?’ is omitted: if Shuʿayb truly has clear proof and prophethood, he must command them to abandon idols and sins, as that is why prophets are sent.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الكلام يناوي عليه، والمعنى أخبروني إن كنت على حجة واضحة ويقين من ربي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan says calling the proposed clause the answer to ‘Have you considered?’ is not technical: it is the second object of the verb when it means ‘inform me.’
rows.anchor: وتسمية هذا جوابا لأرأيتم ليس بالمصطلح، بل هذه الجملة التي قدرها هي في موضع المفعول الثاني

rows.speaker: الحوفي
rows.claim: Al-Hawfi says the conditional answer is omitted and estimates: would I turn away from my worship on this basis?
rows.anchor: وقال الحوفي: وجواب الشرط محذوف لدلالة الكلام عليه

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya estimates the omitted conditional answer as ‘would I go astray as you have,’ or abandon delivering the message, or a similar response fitting the argument.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: وجواب الشرط الذي في قوله: إن كنت على بينة من ربي محذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects ‘I would go astray’ as the conditional answer: if declarative, it does not follow from the condition; if interrogative with an omitted hamza, it is the second object of ‘Have you considered?’
rows.anchor: وليس قوله: أضل جوابا للشرط، لأنه إن كان مثبتا فلا يمكن أن يكون جوابا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Good provision’ apparently means lawful, wholesome wealth acquired without short measure or fraud.
rows.anchor: والظاهر في قوله: رزقا حسنا أنه الحلال الطيب من غير بخس ولا تطفيف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas glosses ‘good provision’ as lawful wealth; Shuʿayb had abundant wealth.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: الحلال، وكان شعيب عليه السلام كثير المال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other interpretations of ‘good provision’ are prophethood or knowledge.
rows.anchor: وكان شعيب عليه السلام كثير المال. وقيل: النبوة. وقيل: العلم

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya explains that Shuʿayb does not intend to do the short-measuring and weight-cheating he forbids, then monopolize the money.
rows.anchor: من نقص الكيل والوزن وأستأثر بالمال قاله: ابن عطية

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says Shuʿayb would not forbid an action and then commit it himself.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: لم أكن لأنهاكم عن أمر ثم أرتكبه

rows.speaker: صاحب الغنيان
rows.claim: The author of al-Ghunyān understands the phrase as refusing to do privately what Shuʿayb forbids publicly.
rows.anchor: وقال صاحب الغنيان: ما أريد أن أخالفكم في السر إلى ما أنهاكم عنه في العلانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In usage, ‘he opposed me toward it’ means he headed toward something while I turned away; ‘he opposed me away from it’ means the reverse, illustrated by travelers meeting at water.
rows.anchor: ويقال: خالفني فلان إلى كذا إذا قصده وأنت مول عنه، وخالفني عنه إذا ولى عنه وأنت قاصده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sense is that Shuʿayb would get ahead of them in the desires he forbids and reserve them for himself; grammatically, ‘that I oppose you’ may be the object of ‘I want,’ with khālafa meaning ‘followed behind.’
rows.anchor: والمعنى أن أسبقكم إلى شهواتكم التي نهيتكم عنها لأستبد بها دونكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One analysis makes ‘toward’ attach to ‘oppose,’ or to an omitted phrase meaning ‘inclined toward what I forbid.’
rows.anchor: وتتعلق إلى بأخالفكم، أو بمحذوف أي: مائلا إلى ما أنهاكم عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another analysis retains the apparent sense of opposition and supplies ‘inclined toward’; alternatively, the clause is a purpose complement, with ‘toward’ attached to ‘I want.’
rows.anchor: أو يبقى أن أخالفكم على ظاهر ما يفهم من المخالفة، ويكون في موضع المفعول به بأريد

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj reads the phrase as ‘I do not intend, by opposing you, to undertake what I forbid you.’
rows.anchor: ولذلك قال الزجاج: وما أقصد بخلافكم إلى ارتكاب ما أنهاكم عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘As long as I can’ is apparently a time clause: for as long as Shuʿayb can reform, he will spare no effort.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن ما مصدرية ظرفية أي مدة استطاعتي للإصلاح، وما دمت متمكنا منه لا آلوا فيه جهدا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari offers two analyses of ‘except reform as much as I can’: it may replace ‘reform,’ or include an omitted noun, ‘reform of what I can.’
rows.anchor: وأجاز الزمخشري في ما وجوها أحدها: أن يكون بدلا من الإصلاح

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari's third analysis makes the phrase an object, as in a poetic example: Shuʿayb seeks only to repair as much of their corruption as he can.
rows.anchor: والثالث: أن يكون مفعولا كقوله: ضعيف النكاية أعداءه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan calls that third analysis weak: Kufans disallow a definite verbal noun with al- from governing a direct object, and Basrans allow it only rarely.
rows.anchor: وهذا الثالث ضعيف، لأن المصدر المعرف بأل لا يجوز إعماله في المفعول به عند الكوفيين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘My success’ means either divine aid for calling them to worship God alone and avoid what He forbids, or aid in keeping one's actions rightly aligned with God's pleasure.
rows.anchor: وما توفيقي أي لدعائكم إلى عبادة الله وحده، وترك ما نهاكم عنه إلا بمعونة الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His reliance is on God alone and to Him he returns in all speech and action; this asks for divine support, threatens disbelievers, and removes their hope of harming him.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا طلب التأييد من الله تعالى، وتهديد للكفار وحسم لأطماعهم أن ينالوه بشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Do not let my opposition cause you’ means do not let my disagreement and hostility bring harm upon you.
rows.anchor: ومعنى لا يجرمنكم: لا يكسبنكم شقاقي، أي خلافي وعداوتي

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi explains the opposition as each side being on a different side.
rows.anchor: قال السدي: كأنه في شق وهم في شق

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan glosses it as ‘my hardship,’ deriving it from the sense of difficulty.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: ضراري جعله من المشقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the word to mean ‘my separation.’
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: ضراري جعله من المشقة. وقيل: فراقي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The forms jaramtu and kasabtu take two objects, as in ‘I made Zayd commit the sin’ and ‘I made Zayd acquire money.’
rows.anchor: ويتعدى إلى اثنين جرمت زيدا الذنب، وكسبت زيدا المال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the hamza form, jarama still takes two objects; Abu Hayyan refers readers to his earlier discussion in al-ʿUqūd.
rows.anchor: وبالألف يتعدى إلى اثنين أيضا، أجرم زيد عمرا الذنب

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid, al-Jahdari, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and a report from Nafiʿ read mathala with an open lām; Abu Hayyan gives two grammatical parses.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مجاهد، والجحدري، وابن أبي إسحاق، ورويت عن نافع: مثل بفتح اللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the first parse, the open vowel is a building vowel: the word remains a nominative subject, with a permitted construct ending when attached to a non-declinable word.
rows.anchor: أحدهما: أن تكون الفتحة فتحة بناء، وهو فاعل كحاله حين كان مرفوعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the second parse, mathala is an accusative adjective for an omitted verbal noun: ‘a punishment like the punishment of Noah's people’; the understood subject is the punishment.
rows.anchor: والثاني: أن تكون الفتحة فتحة إعراب، وانتصب على أنه نعت لمصدر محذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The construction is compared with the reading ‘it is true, just as you speak,’ from 51:23.
rows.anchor: كقراءة من قرأ إنه لحق مثل ما أنكم تنطقون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lut's people were ‘not far’ either in time, because their destruction was recent and they were the nearest people destroyed, or in their unbelief and sins deserving destruction.
rows.anchor: وما قوم لوط منكم ببعيد، إما في الزمان لقرب عهد هلاكهم من عهدكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Far’ can describe them by time or place, stand for an omitted ‘thing,’ or refer elliptically to the destruction of Lut's people.
rows.anchor: وأجرى بعيدا على قوم إما باعتبار الزمان أو المكان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic may use singular masculine near/far, much/little, and friend for plural or feminine subjects, as in the examples of one or many friends.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يسوى في قريب وبعيد وكثير وقليل بين المفرد والجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wadūd is an intensive form on faʿūl from wadda, ‘to love and prefer’; al-Kisa'i heard wadidtu with a fatḥa, and the verbal nouns include wudd, widād, and widāda.
rows.anchor: وودود بناء مبالغة من ود الشيء أحبه وآثره، وهو على فعل

rows.speaker: بعض أهل اللغة
rows.claim: Some linguists allow wadūd as a faʿūl form with passive meaning, ‘beloved.’
rows.anchor: وقال بعض أهل اللغة: يجوز أن يكون ودود فعول بمعنى مفعول

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Exegetes gloss Wadūd as God showing affection to His servants through beneficence, or as beloved by believers; His mercy and love lead them to seek forgiveness and repent, since without it He would not guide them to do so.
rows.anchor: وقال المفسرون: ودود متحبب إلى عباده بالإحسان إليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase ‘we do not understand much of what you say’ may mean they would not listen attentively out of aversion, as in 6:25.
rows.anchor: لا يصغون لكلامه رغبة عنه وكراهة له كقوله تعالى: وجعلنا على قلوبهم أكنة أن يفقهوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They may have understood Shuʿayb but refused to accept him, behaving as though they had not understood.
rows.anchor: أو كانوا يفهمونه ولكنهم لم يقبلوه، فكأنهم لم يفقهوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They may have said ‘we do not understand’ to show disdain, like someone dismissing another's words.
rows.anchor: أو قالوا ذلك على وجه الاستهانة به كما يقول الرجل لصاحبه إذا لم يعبأ بحديثه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They may have called his speech incoherent, but Abu Hayyan says it was among the most eloquent and clear speech, understandable even to slower minds; God had willed to abandon them.
rows.anchor: وكيف لا يتفهم كلامه وهو خطيب الأنبياء عليهم الصلاة والسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Weak’ apparently means Shuʿayb lacked strength and standing among them, so he could not defend himself if they wanted to harm him.
rows.anchor: ومعنى ضعيفا: لا قوة لك ولا عز فيما بيننا، فلا تقدر على الامتناع منا

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan glosses ‘weak’ as humiliated.
rows.anchor: لا قوة لك ولا عز فيما بيننا، فلا تقدر على الامتناع منا إن أردناك بمكروه، وعن الحسن: ضعيفا مهينا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says Shuʿayb was thin-bodied, making him unimpressive; Arabs admired large bodies and disparaged ugliness.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كان ناحل البدن زمنه لا يقع في القلب منه هيبة ولا في العين منه امتلاء

rows.speaker: الباقر
rows.claim: Al-Baqir interprets ‘weak’ as shunned, with no one sitting or socializing with him.
rows.anchor: وقال الباقر: مهجورا لا تجالس ولا تعاشر

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says ‘weak’ means Shuʿayb's clan had not believed in him.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: ضعيفا أي لم يؤمن بك رهطك

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi interprets ‘weak’ as alone in his doctrine and belief.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: وحيدا في مذهبك واعتقادك

rows.speaker: ابن جبير وشريك القاضي
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr and Sharik al-Qadi say Shuʿayb was blind; al-Zuhrawi and al-Zamakhshari report that Himyar used ‘weak’ for a blind person.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جبير وشريك القاضي: ضعيفا ضرير البصر أعمى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan finds the Himyar usage unlikely here, given the other explanation of blindness or the alternatives of thinness and weak sight; the apparent meaning is inability to defend himself.
rows.anchor: ويبعده تفسيره هنا بأعمى أو بناحل البدن أو بضعيف البصر كما قاله الثوري

rows.speaker: أبو روق
rows.claim: Abu Rawq claims God never sent a blind prophet or one with a chronic infirmity.
rows.anchor: وزعم أبو روق: أن الله لم يبعث نبيا أعمى، ولا نبيا به زمانة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan prefers the apparent meaning: Shuʿayb was weak in power and ability to defend himself.
rows.anchor: بل الظاهر أنه ضعيف الانتصار والقدرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They spared Shuʿayb because they respected his clan, who were unbelievers like them, or because the clan had strength and protection; otherwise they would stone him.
rows.anchor: احترموه لرهطه إذ كانوا كفارا مثلهم، أو كان في عزة ومنعة منهم

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd takes ‘we would stone you’ literally, as death by stones, one of the worst killings.
rows.anchor: ظاهره القتل بالحجارة، وهي من شر القتلات، وبه قال ابن زيد

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari says it means verbal abuse, a usage also found in Arab speech and poetry.
rows.anchor: وقال الطبري: رجمناك بالسب، وهذا أيضا تستعمله العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that they would banish Shuʿayb and expel him from their land.
rows.anchor: وقيل: لأبعدناك وأخرجناك من أرضنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘You are not dear to us’ means they did not honor Shuʿayb enough to refrain from killing him; only his clan mattered to them because it shared their religion.
rows.anchor: أي: لا تعز ولا تكرم حتى نكرمك من القتل، ونرفعك عن الرجم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other glosses of ‘dear’ are possessing protection, high standing in their eyes, dominance, or kingship, since they called a king ʿAzīz.
rows.anchor: وقيل: بعزيز بذي منعة، وعزة منزلة في نفوسنا. وقيل: بذي غلبة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says placing the pronoun before negation makes the statement concern Shuʿayb himself, not an action: he is not dear, while his clan is; contempt for God's prophet is contempt for God, as 4:80 says obedience to the Messenger is obedience to God.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: وقد دل إيلاء ضميره حرف النفي على أن الكلام واقع في الفاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in ‘you took it behind your backs’ apparently refers to God: they forgot Him and treated Him like something cast aside and ignored.
rows.anchor: تعالى أي: ونسيتموه وجعلتموه كالشيء المنبوذ وراء الظهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form ẓihriyy is a genitive relation to ẓahr with an altered ending, like ʾimsiyy from ʾams.
rows.anchor: والظهري بكسر الظاء منسوب إلى الظهر من تغييرات النسب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although they spoke harshly, Shuʿayb answers with tenderness, consistent with his gentle manner: God deserves more regard than the clan, and Shuʿayb is more entitled to be regarded for God's sake.
rows.anchor: ولما خاطبوه خطاب الإهانة والجفاء جريا على عادة الكفار مع أنبيائهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view makes the pronoun refer to the law Shuʿayb brought.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الضمير في واتخذتموه به عائد على الشرع الذي جاء شعيب عليه السلام

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad takes ẓihriyy as support or something used for strength, and understands them to have used disobedience to fend Shuʿayb off, with an omitted possessive construction.
rows.anchor: قال المبرد: فالمعنى واتخذتم العصيان عنده لدفعي

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya cites a view that they made God their support and the foundation of their hopes.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: وقالت فرقة: واتخذتموه أي وأنتم متخذون الله سند ظهوركم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority view is that Shuʿayb's people denied and knew nothing of God; the alternative says they acknowledged the Creator and Provider but treated idols as intermediaries.
rows.anchor: فقول الجمهور: على أن كفر قوم شعيب كان جحدا بالله وجهلا به

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says ẓihriyy means surplus, like spare camels kept in case they are needed.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: الظهري الفضل، مثل الحمال يخرج معه بإبل ظهارية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's encompassing their deeds means nothing is hidden from Him and carries a warning and threat.
rows.anchor: محيط أحاط بأعمالكم فلا يخفى عليه شيء منها، وفي ضمنه توعد وتهديد

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ and al-Zamakhshari allow ‘who will receive it’ to be a relative clause object of ‘you will know,’ identifying the wretched person punished and the liar.
rows.anchor: وجوز الفراء، والزمخشري: في من يأتيه أن تكون موصولة مفعولة بقوله: تعلمون

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: They also allow it to be an interrogative subject, with ‘you will know’ suspended: which of us will be punished, and which is the liar?
rows.anchor: واستفهامية في موضع رفع على الابتداء، وتعلمون معلق كأنه قيل: أينا يأتيه عذاب

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya prefers the relative-clause analysis, arguing that an interrogative cannot be connected by a relative link.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: والأول أحسن، يعني كونها مفعولة قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects Ibn ʿAtiyya's reasoning: the clause need not be relative and may be an interrogative coordinated with the interrogative ‘who is a liar?’
rows.anchor: إذ لا يتعين أن تكون موصولة لا محالة كما قال، بل تكون استفهامية

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says the fāʾ explicitly links the warning, while its omission creates an implicit connection by answering an unstated question; he calls resumption the stronger and more eloquent link.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: (فإن قلت) : أي فرق بين إدخال الفاء ونزعها في سوف تعلمون؟ (قلت) :

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says ‘who is a liar’ matches their accusation of Shuʿayb and thereby exposes their ignorance, although the expected parallel would name the truthful prophet.
rows.anchor: ولكنهم لما كانوا يعدونه كاذبا قال: ومن هو كاذب يعني في زعمكم ودعواكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan calls al-Zamakhshari's wording disrespectful and rejects his grammatical argument: the threat concerns only them, not the Prophet, and the preceding and following context confirms this.
rows.anchor: وفي ألفاظ هذا الرجل سوء أدب، والذي قاله ليس بقياس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parallel in 39:40 likewise threatens the people addressed by ‘act according to your position’; it does not include the prophet in the threat.
rows.anchor: ونظيره في سورة تنزيل: فسوف تعلمون من يأتيه عذاب يخزيه ويحل عليه عذاب مقيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Wait’ means await the outcome and what Shuʿayb says; raqīb can mean a vigilant watcher, one who watches alongside another, or one who waits, fitting the reciprocal command to wait.
rows.anchor: وارتقبوا: انتظروا العاقبة، وما أقول لكم. والرقيب بمعنى الراقب فعيل للمبالغة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari explains that the middle narratives use fāʾ because they follow the promised morning and result from it; the stories of ʿAd and Midian begin separately and take wāw as one story follows another.
rows.anchor: قد وقعت الوسطيان بعد ذكر الوعد وذلك قوله: إن موعدهم الصبح ذلك وعد غير مكذوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Sulami and Abu Haywa read baʿudat with ḍamma for distance opposite nearness, while most readers use kasra; Arabs distinguish distance associated with destruction by changing the form, and the ḍamma reading follows the general sense.
rows.anchor: وقرأ السلمي وأبو حيوة: كما بعدت بضم العين من البعد الذي هو ضد القرب

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba distinguishes baʿuda for distance ending in destruction from baʿida for ‘came to me.’
rows.anchor: وقال ابن قتيبة: بعد يبعد إذا كان بعده هلكة، وبعد يبعد إذا أتاني

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Nahhas says the established usage baʿuda ya-baʿudu means to perish.
rows.anchor: وقال النحاس: المعروف في اللغة بعد يبعد بعدا وبعدا إذا هلك

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawi says baʿida can describe good or evil, while baʿuda is restricted to evil.
rows.anchor: وقال المهدوي: بعد يستعمل في الخير والشر، وبعد في الشر خاصة

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari says some Arabs use both verb forms for both destruction and ordinary distance.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأنباري: من العرب من يسوي بين الهلاك والبعد الذي هو ضد القرب

rows.speaker: مالك بن الريب
rows.claim: Malik ibn al-Rayb's line uses baʿuda to mean ‘perished.’
rows.anchor: وقال مالك بن الريب: في بعد بمعنى هلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The imperative baʿd for a person is a curse meaning ‘be removed’; it is used only against an enemy, as in ‘away with the unbelievers.’
rows.anchor: وبعد الفلان دعاء عليه، ولا يدعى به إلا على مبغض كقولك: سحقا للكافرين

rows.speaker: أهل علم البيان
rows.claim: Rhetoricians call this the Quran's only instance of istitrād: beginning with praise or blame, then ending with the original aim; Hassan's poem about al-Harith ibn Hisham illustrates it.
rows.anchor: وقال أهل علم البيان: لم يرد في القرآن استطراد إلا هذا الموضع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs given to Moses were nine: staff, hand, flood, locusts, lice, frogs, blood, and decreases in wealth, lives, and fruits; some replace the decrease with the mountain's overshadowing.
rows.anchor: الآيات المعجزات التسع: العصا، واليد، والطوفان، والجراد، والقمل، والضفادع، والدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The view that the signs were the Torah is unsound because it was revealed after Pharaoh and his chiefs perished.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الآيات التوراة، وهذا ليس بسديد، لأنه قال إلى فرعون وملائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clear authority may mean the clear proofs within the signs, which show Moses' truth, or the staff singled out as the most striking sign, like Gabriel and Michael singled out after the angels.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يريد بها العصا لأنها أبهر تلك الآيات، فنص عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's command apparently means his order to disbelieve and deny Moses' miracles; it may also mean his path or affair.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن يراد بقوله: أمر فرعون أمره إياهم بالكفر وجحد معجزات موسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling Pharaoh's command not rightly guided exposes the ignorance of those who followed him: he claimed divinity despite being human, and they saw Moses' signs and truth but left him for a leader without guidance.
rows.anchor: وما أمر فرعون برشيد: نفى عنه الرشد، وذلك تجهيل لمتبعيه حيث شايعوه على أمره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rashīd may mean rightly guided, or a guide directing people toward good.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون رشيد بمعنى راشد، ويكون رشيد بمعنى مرشد أي بمرشد إلى خير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh denied a creator and resurrection and taught each land's people to obey their ruler, so his command was entirely devoid of right guidance.
rows.anchor: وكان فرعون دهريا نافيا للصانع والمعاد، وكان يقول: لا إله للعالم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rashd denotes whatever is praised and approved; its opposite is ghayy.
rows.anchor: والرشد يستعمل في كل ما يحمد ويرتضى، والغي ضده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh goes ahead of his drowned people into the Fire; as their model in misguidance, he leads them there and they follow.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: أنه يقدم قومه المغرقين إلى النار، وكما كان قدوة في الضلال متبعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rashīd may mean a praiseworthy outcome; ‘he leads his people’ then explains the result and shows how his command could not be good.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون قوله: برشيد بحميد، العاقبة، ويكون قوله: يقدم قومه، تفسيرا لذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shift from ‘he would lead them’ to the past ‘he led them’ presents the outcome as certain and intensifies the warning; alternatively, he brought them to the Fire in this life, meaning disbelief.
rows.anchor: وعدل عن فيوردهم إلى فأوردهم لتحقق وقوعه لا محالة، فكأنه قد وقع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The worldly-fire interpretation is remote because the fāʾ and the word wurūd here point to actually entering the Fire of abiding, not merely approaching it, as in Moses reaching Midian's water in 28:23.
rows.anchor: ويبعد هذا التأويل الفاء والورود في هذه الآية. ورود الخلود وليس بورود الإشراف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The destination ‘Fire’ may be governed by the second of the two competing verbs, ‘he leads’ and ‘he brought them to it,’ with the first verb's complement omitted.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن تكون النار تصيبه على إعمال الثاني لأنه تنازعه يقدم أي: إلى النار وفأوردهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hamza in awrada is causative: warada takes one object, while the causative takes two, the person brought and the destination.
rows.anchor: والهمزة في فأوردهم للتعدية، ورد يتعدى إلى واحد، فلما أدخلت الهمزة تعدى إلى اثنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wird can denote the one who arrives, so the phrase needs an ellipsis to match the blamed subject: ‘how evil is the place of arrival—the Fire.’
rows.anchor: ويطلق الورد على الوارد، فالورد لا يكون المورود، فاحتيج إلى حذف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parsing of al-mawrūd may follow the same options as Zayd in ‘bad is the man, Zayd.’
rows.anchor: ويجوز في إعراب المورود ما يجوز في زيد من قولك: بئس الرجل زيد

rows.speaker: ابن عطية وأبو البقاء
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya and Abu al-Baqaʾ allow al-mawrūd to modify al-wird, with the condemned item omitted and understood as the Fire; this depends on allowing an adjective for the subject of biʾsa.
rows.anchor: وجوز ابن عطية وأبو البقاء أن يكون المورود صفة للورد

rows.speaker: ابن السراج والفارسي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sarraj and al-Farisi disallow an adjective modifying the subject of niʿma or biʾsa.
rows.anchor: ذهب ابن السراج والفارسي إلى أن ذلك لا يجوز

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari compares Pharaoh to the water scout who goes ahead of a caravan and his followers to the arriving caravan; Hell is an evil destination because a watering place should quench thirst, whereas Fire does the opposite.
rows.anchor: وشبه اتباعه بالواردة، ثم قيل: بئس الورد الذي يردونه النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari's gloss makes al-mawrūd an adjective and leaves the condemned destination, the Fire, implicit; this also relies on allowing the subject of biʾsa to take an adjective.
rows.anchor: يدل على أن المورود صفة للورد، وأن المخصوص بالذم محذوف، ولذلك قدره النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative parses the phrase as ‘evil are the people brought,’ with wird meaning the arriving group and an omitted pronoun as the target of blame; it condemns the people rather than the place.
rows.anchor: وقيل: التقدير بئس القوم المورود بهم هم، فيكون الورد عني به الجمع الوارد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘In this’ refers to the present world, as the Hud account makes explicit; ‘the Day of Resurrection’ denotes the next world and coordinates with the phrase's syntactic position, so they receive a curse in both.
rows.anchor: والإشارة بقوله: في هذه إلى الدنيا وقد جاء مصرحا بها في قصة هود

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says their worldly curse comes from believers or by drowning, while the Resurrection curse comes from angels or the Fire.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: في هذه لعنة من المؤمنين أو بالغرق، ويوم القيامة من الملائكة أو بالنار

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says they receive two curses.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: فلهم لعنتان، وذهب قوم إلى أن التقسيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say they receive one curse in this world and, at the Resurrection, an evil reward rather than another curse.
rows.anchor: وذهب قوم إلى أن التقسيم هو أن لهم في الدنيا لعنة، ويوم القيامة يرفدون به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects that reading because it makes ‘the Day of Resurrection’ depend on biʾsa, which is invariable and cannot have its complement placed before it; it would work if postponed.
rows.anchor: وهذا لا يصح لأن هذا التأويل يدل على أن يوم القيامة معمول لبئس، وبئس لا يتصرف
